items.html: The house gets an admin, and Tunebox reaches past the browser. One password runs the place, your own files play beside YouTube, and a terminal can do everything the page does.

One admin password for the house. It opens a panel to edit, merge, block and remove people, and to clean up plays, likes and playlists. It locks again after 15 minutes left alone, and a run of wrong passwords locks it for everyone for a while.
Every admin change is written down in a log the admin can read.
Playlists have owners.
A forgotten admin password can be reset on the server itself, with run.py --reset-admin.
A backup made without the admin leaves the pass phrases out. Restoring one, and signing in to YouTube, need the admin.

Feature switches. The admin can switch off names, groups, playlists, likes, Home and Explore, pasted links, the radio, lyrics, Stats, the recap, the wall screen, the alarm, the sleep timer, the equaliser, local songs, the theme and accent pickers, and the names in Settings. What is off is hidden for everyone, and nothing is deleted.
Presets set the switches in one go: Home, Office, Party and Solo.
A House tab for the house’s name, accent and time zone, sign-ups, groups with any name and the house’s own word for them, and the wall screen’s options.
A blocklist for songs and artists. A blocked song cannot be added, and the radio and the queue drop it.
Upload your own audio files on a Local page, with a button or by dropping them, with progress for each file. They play, queue, like and count like any other song.
Tags and covers are read from the files, and can be edited.
WAV and AIFF are kept as FLAC, and unusual formats as Opus.
Search shows local matches first. The radio after a local song plays YouTube’s copy of the same song, or the other local songs.
The admin’s Local tab shows the disk use, a cap, the free space to keep and the biggest file, and makes a full backup as a zip with the audio in it.

The tunebox command does what the page does, from a terminal: what is playing, adding by words, link or id, the controls, the queue, search, playlists, likes, stats, the admin and the rest. install.sh puts it on the server, and tunebox.bat starts it on Windows.

tunebox tui is the whole player full-screen in a terminal, with tabs for Home, Search, Queue, Playlists, History, Local, Stats, Lyrics, Settings and the admin, and Up next beside the player on a wide window. --ascii and NO_COLOR work.
The player line in the terminal no longer jumps back when a slow answer arrives late.

The radio carries on from the added song that plays last, not from the newest one added. Play next, Play now and a song taking its turn in the middle leave it alone. Removing, moving or blocking the last song moves it along.
The wall screen dims to its clock after 30 seconds paused, where it waited two minutes.

Panels slide out the way they came in, and a finger can drag them away. Drawers, pop-ups and the menu sheet follow the finger, and Now playing rises from the mini bar and goes back down. A flick counts as much as the distance.
A removed queue row keeps going and the rest close up, and a dropped row travels to its place. Every button answers a press at once, and the menu grows from where you pressed.
Reduced motion fades instead of switching everything off.
On a phone, the volume button opens a small volume bar over the player, not Settings.
A tap on the big cover shows the lyrics, and a swipe sideways skips.
The name form takes the whole screen on a phone.
Now playing holds a steady frame rate on a phone. The blurred cover behind it waits until the screen stops moving.
Hover colours no longer stick to the last button tapped on a touch screen.
A pop-up’s buttons stay above the keyboard in Firefox and Safari.
Names are big tiles, yours first with a ring around it, so most houses fit without scrolling.
Find your name in a search box that ignores accents and matches groups too, or filter by group with a row of chips. When nothing matches, one tap adds what you typed as a new name.
A padlock on a name says it has a pass phrase before you tap it.
Listening as sits at the top with an Edit link, in place of Edit my profile.
A new group is made with + New in the name form.
Performance mode for devices with little power: no movement, blur or shadows, and fewer requests to the server. Auto turns it on for a slow device.
A Network section shows the address other devices open Tunebox at, with a Copy button, and the Wi-Fi to join. The admin can type the Wi-Fi’s name, or the server’s own is shown.
The address is right with a VPN on. It is the server’s address on the same network as the device asking.
Names wear drawn icons, and a pass phrase shows a drawn padlock.
Search results offer Play only. Play next is still in Play’s question and in the song’s menu.

Fun stats: skips, songs cut short with Play now, and awards for the house - The DJ, On repeat, Itchy finger, Can’t wait, Tough crowd, Night owl and Explorer. One person’s Stats and recap show their own habits instead.
On this day, a row on Home with what the house played on this date a year ago, or a month ago.
A song’s menu says how often the house played it, since when, and whose song it mostly is.
Stats download as a spreadsheet: Download as CSV gives every play in the period on screen.
Home opens with songs. Your own rows come first, then a new Recommended row from a song played lately, then YouTube’s song rows. Mixes and albums follow.
Top 30, next to Liked songs: the house’s most played songs of the last 30 days, with how often each played. It keeps itself up to date.
Find and sort inside a playlist by title or artist, once it has more than a few songs.
Select several songs in Up next or a playlist, then play them next, add them to a playlist or take them out in one go.
Recent searches show under the empty search box, one tap to search again.
Not for the radio: anyone can tell the radio to stop picking a song from its menu. It can still be added by hand, and the admin can bring it back.
Songs without a cover get a drawn one, headphones, a record or a note, the same one every time.
Local sits between Playlists and History in the menu.
A short last row of tiles no longer leaves a grey block beside it.
Every queued song says when it plays, and the player bar says when your next one is up.
Mine shows only your songs in Up next, with Take mine out.
Adding a song that is already waiting asks first.
A queued song shows who added it by name beside their icon, in place of their groups.
The number on the queue button counts only queued songs, not the radio’s.
A tap on a synced lyric line plays from there at once, on the wall too.
Now playing loads the cover at full size.
A bar along the top says when the server can’t be reached, and the buttons rest until it is back.

A new background, after Nothing OS 5’s: big soft lights and a few soft discs in the cover’s colours float slowly about, under hairline circles and dashed lines that drift too, and a fine grain. Each song has its own, the same every time it plays, and the shapes glide into their new places when the song changes.
The cover takes gestures: tap its left or right half for the previous or next song, double-tap to like, drag up or down for the volume.
Add songs from the wall: the magnifying glass at the top right opens a big search. Songs added there are the house’s, not anyone’s, and Stats counts them.
The lyrics scroll with a finger or the wheel, and pick up the line being sung again a few seconds later.
The cover, title and buttons sit in one centred column.
A button shows or hides the lyrics on that wall, and the full screen button steps aside while the wall is full screen.
Leaving the wall takes four presses of the X at the top right, so a stray tap doesn’t close it.
A join code under the idle clock and in the search: guests scan it to open Tunebox on their phone.
Night hours, set by the admin: the wall dims to the clock and the song.
The picture drifts a few pixels every two minutes, so a TV left on all day does not burn in.
Bigger targets for fingers on a touch screen.
Quiet hours: in the hours set, nobody can turn the volume above the limit, and a louder volume comes down to it.
Here now, in the People tab: every device with Tunebox open, and the name it picked.
A backup every night, kept for 14 nights on the server.
tunebox now --short prints the song for a shell prompt or a status bar.
tunebox tray puts Tunebox in the Windows notification area, and the keyboard’s media keys play, pause and skip on the house’s speakers.
Maintenance: deploying goes to any server, from a list kept on each computer, and save.sh does it from macOS and Linux.
Tunebox grows up. A Now playing screen, groups and pass phrases, Stats and a recap, and it runs on any computer, not only the house server.

A Now playing screen: the big cover on a blurred copy of itself, with the song, a like, the controls, volume, lyrics and Up next. On a phone it opens from the mini bar with a tap or a swipe up. On a desktop, click the song in the bar, or press N.
A mini bar on a phone with the cover, the title, a like, play and a thin progress line. Swipe it sideways to skip.
Play and pause fade over half a second, on every page and the wall screen at once.
Every Lyrics button shows the lyrics beside the cover while Now playing is open.

Tunebox asks before interrupting. While a song is on, a tap on a song, an album’s Play or a shelf asks: play it now, play it next, or add it to the end of the queue. Play next and Add all still act at once.

Right-click for a menu on a song, a card, a page header, the player or the queue, or press and hold on a touch screen: play, play next, add to the end, add to a playlist, like, go to the artist or the album, copy the link.
Artist and album names link to their pages, and Back walks back through them.
A change to the equaliser is heard at once. It waited for the next pause.
A new audio quality applies at once, not after a restart.
A player crash in the middle of a fade no longer leaves the volume turned down.
Home, Explore and moods say what went wrong when YouTube fails.
One interface. Classic is gone, and its old addresses open the player.
Groups. Everyone belongs to at least one, with three letters and a colour, shown beside the name in the queue, the history and People.
A name can have a pass phrase. A device types it once and keeps a key; without it the name cannot be used or edited. Add, change or remove it from People in Settings.
The names list and the name form are apart, and the form shows a live preview of the badge. Edit my profile is in the Who’s listening menu.
Liked songs shows who liked each song, and filters by person or group. So does the Liked mix on Home.
Two quick taps without a name ask who is listening once, not twice.
Every play is kept: the song, who added it, radio or not, and the seconds actually heard.

A Stats page, on T, for any period, the house, a person or a group: minutes, plays, songs, artists, new songs, the best streak, top songs and artists, who added the most, the time of day and the day of the week.
The recap: story slides for any period, person or group, opened from Stats, ending with Play the top songs.
Backup and restore in Settings: one file with everything the house made except the YouTube sign-in. A restore keeps what it replaced.
Tunebox can be installed as an app, with its own icon.
Tunebox runs on any computer. start.bat on Windows and start.sh on Linux fetch what is missing the first time, and install.sh sets up a Linux server.
The alarm works on Python 3.14 and on Windows.
Text no longer selects on clicks and drags. Fields still do.
Maintenance: the code was split into parts, and Tunebox moved out of homeapps into its own repository.
Tunebox learns who is listening. Names, a queue that takes turns, the house’s own shelves on Home, and a screen for the wall.
Who’s listening. Everyone picks a name once per device, with a colour and an icon, and the queue and the history show who added each song. Likes stay shared, and remember who liked them.
A queue in two parts: the songs people added, taking turns between them, then the radio, which follows the last song added.
Play next and Play now on every song, and Play, Play next and Add all on albums, playlists and the history.
Undo any change to the queue from a toast, from the queue, or with Z, and go back to an earlier queue from a list.
On a touch screen, swipe a queue row left to remove it, right to play it next, and drag it by its grip.
For you shelves on Home: Most played in the last 30 days, Liked mix and House mix. Explore shows new albums, and moods and genres.
Paste a YouTube or YouTube Music link into search to open its album, playlist, artist or song.
The wall screen at /wall, for a tablet or a TV: the cover, synced lyrics, big controls, and a dimmed clock when nothing plays.
A Settings button in Up next.
Up next keeps a tap that lands while it updates, and the radio stays after Clear, with a Start radio button.
A page that finishes loading after you moved on no longer takes over.
A cover that fails to load shows an empty tile, not a broken image.
